historical_timeline.summary: Invalided home from the Discovery expedition after breathlessness and weakness on the southern journey.
On the Nimrod expedition, very unwell after pulling on a rope; a pulmonary systolic murmur heard.
Endurance expedition; three men of the Ross Sea party died.
Organized the Shackleton-Rowett expedition in London.
Sudden faintness ashore at Rio de Janeiro.
Died aboard the Quest at Grytviken; Macklin recorded atheroma of the coronary arteries.

claims.statement: Ernest Henry Shackleton was born on February 15, 1874, at Kilkea, County Kildare, Ireland, the son of Dr. Henry Shackleton, of a well-known Quaker family.

source_links.locator: born at Kilkea, Co. Kildare, in 1874; son of Dr. Henry Shackleton

claims.statement: On the southern sledge journey of the Discovery expedition he became unable to pull the sledge because of breathlessness and weakness; the collapse was attributed to scurvy and "a sort of asthma," and he was invalided home against his will in 1903.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Documented exertional breathlessness in his late twenties. Its cause is disputed (CLM-0010, CLM-0011).

source_links.locator: inflamed gums, severe dyspnea, exercise intolerance
Macklin: the scurvy of the southern journey of the Discovery expedition

claims.statement: On the Nimrod expedition (1907 to 1909), its medical officer Eric Marshall recorded in his diary on January 20, 1908, that Shackleton was very unwell after pulling on a rope, and twice heard a pulmonary systolic murmur.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Documented exertional illness and a heart murmur in his thirties; the cause is disputed.

claims.statement: On the Imperial Trans-Antarctic (Endurance) expedition of 1914 to 1917, of fifty-six men three died in the Antarctic: Mackintosh, Hayward, and Spencer-Smith of the Ross Sea party. No member of the Endurance's own party died.
claims.clinical_interpretation: After this, he wrote South, published in 1919; not a clinical claim.

source_links.locator: final chapter: three died in the Antarctic, all of the Ross Sea party

claims.statement: His colleague Dr. James McIlroy later recalled that on one occasion Shackleton would not undress and let him listen to his heart.
claims.clinical_interpretation: A recollection quoted in a later essay; the year is not used. Anchors the modern episode's reluctance to be examined, which is worked through by shared decision-making.

claims.statement: He was a heavy cigarette smoker for most of his life.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Stated by the authors of a 2016 essay on his heart; the synthetic smoking history is anchored to it.

claims.statement: After the war he returned to London. In 1921, with John Quiller Rowett taking on practically the whole financial responsibility, he turned his planned Arctic expedition into the Shackleton-Rowett expedition to the South; it was organized and equipped within three months, its sailing was postponed beyond August 20 by a strike of ships' joiners and other delays, and the Quest left St. Katharine's Dock in London on September 17, 1921.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Places him in London through the synthetic episode, which ends before the sailing.

source_links.locator: chapter I and the start of chapter II

claims.statement: In Rio de Janeiro, on the morning the Quest sailed in December 1921, an urgent message called Dr. Alexander Macklin to Shackleton, who had been taken suddenly ill ashore; Macklin found him fully recovered, saying he had merely felt a slight faintness. Frank Wild wrote that "this attack had a greater significance than was appreciated at the time." At the end of December, Macklin noticed that he was looking tired and ill.

source_links.locator: chapter III, Rio and the voyage south

claims.statement: At South Georgia, early on January 5, 1922, aboard the Quest at Grytviken, he called Macklin to his cabin, complaining of severe facial neuralgia for which he had taken aspirin; while Macklin was with him he had an attack and died suddenly, at about 2.50 a.m. Macklin wrote that the cause was "atheroma of the coronary arteries," a long-standing condition that in his opinion was due to overstrain during a period of debility. At embalming Macklin could see the heart, but no further pathological examination was feasible.
claims.clinical_interpretation: After the episode. Macklin's wording is documented; the autopsy was not a full pathological examination.

source_links.locator: embalming; angina pectoris with extensive atheroma
died after a heart attack at South Georgia

claims.statement: Two authors argue that his breakdowns, beginning with the Discovery journey, were caused by a congenital atrial septal defect, citing the pulmonary systolic murmur and his episodes of breathlessness and weakness.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective interpretation; the modern echocardiogram shows no shunt and the record does not adopt it.

claims.statement: Other authors propose that the illness on the Discovery expedition was thiamine-deficiency (beriberi) cardiomyopathy, alone or worsened by scurvy.
At the wish of Lady Shackleton he was buried at Grytviken, South Georgia, on March 5, 1922.
claims.clinical_interpretation: After the episode. His wife appears only in this documented claim.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Primary care and cardiology for a 47-year-old expedition leader and heavy smoker with new exertional chest tightness and breathlessness, four months before leading a ship-based polar expedition: pretest probability and risk assessment, a resting ECG and risk-factor tests, coronary CT angiography with CT-FFR as the first test, an echocardiogram, guideline-directed medical therapy (aspirin, high-intensity statin with ezetimibe to an LDL below 55 mg/dL, a beta-blocker, and sublingual nitroglycerin), revascularization when angina persists despite medical therapy and what it does and does not offer in chronic coronary disease, dual antiplatelet therapy, cardiac rehabilitation, varenicline with counseling, the AUDIT with a brief intervention, prediabetes, and fitness for remote high-latitude travel: a symptom-limited exercise test, an evacuation plan, a defibrillator and medicines on board, and cold stress. His reluctance to be examined, and to let anything stop the expedition, is worked through with shared decision-making. Built on the 1918 AHA/ACC chronic coronary disease guideline, the 1919 ESC chronic coronary syndromes guideline, and the CMID ischemic heart disease and hyperlipidemia monographs.

hpi.narrative: Mr. Shackleton returns two weeks after his first visit, on the day of his cardiology consultation with Dr. Solberg-Adebayo, after coronary CT angiography and an echocardiogram this morning. He stopped smoking on his quit date a week ago and is taking varenicline, with mild nausea after the morning dose that eases with food. The chest tightness comes less often on metoprolol, but still comes two or three times a week on the stairs to his office or when he carries a load, and passes within three minutes of rest. He used nitroglycerin twice, with relief within two minutes. He has had no pain at rest, fainting, or palpitations. He is taking aspirin and atorvastatin every day. He has cut down to two drinks on most evenings. He wanted to know whether any of this would be reported to the expedition's backers; he was told it would not, without his consent.

assessment_plan.assessment: The presenting exertional chest tightness now has its cause. Coronary CT angiography this morning shows an 80% stenosis of the proximal left anterior descending artery with a CT-derived fractional flow reserve of 0.70, a 30% plaque in the right coronary artery, and a coronary calcium score of 210. The echocardiogram is normal, with LVEF 58%, normal wall motion and valves, and no interatrial shunt on the agitated-saline study. Angina is less frequent on metoprolol 50 mg but still limits him (Canadian Cardiovascular Society class II). Dr. Solberg-Adebayo recommends a higher beta-blocker dose first and revascularization if angina persists

hpi.narrative: Mr. Shackleton returns four weeks after his consultation. On metoprolol 100 mg his resting pulse is 60, but he still has chest tightness two or three times a week when he climbs the stairs carrying papers or walks fast into a cold wind, and he has used nitroglycerin four times. It never comes at rest. He has not smoked for five weeks. He is drinking within the limit he agreed. He sails in under three months, will be lifting and hauling at sea, and will be weeks from a hospital. He asked whether a stent would let him do that. He was uneasy about having a procedure that the backers might hear of, and said so; after talking it through he wants to go ahead.

assessment_plan.display: Chronic coronary disease with stable angina despite medical therapy
assessment_plan.assessment: Angina persists at class II despite a beta-blocker at a dose that holds his resting pulse at 60, with aspirin and a high-intensity statin. The options were explained: add a long-acting nitrate, amlodipine, or ranolazine; or coronary angiography and a stent to the proximal LAD lesion, which has a CT-FFR of 0.70. In stable coronary disease with normal heart function, a stent relieves angina better than medicines alone but does not lower the risk of heart attack or death. referral.question: Exertional chest tightness and breathlessness for about three months in a 47-year-old heavy smoker who leads a ship-based polar expedition sailing in about four months. Please confirm or exclude obstructive coronary disease, advise on medical therapy and revascularization, and advise whether and how he can safely lead a remote, strenuous, high-latitude expedition
referral.urgency: Within two weeks, with coronary CT angiography before or on the day of the visit
referral.pertinent_history: Chest tightness with breathlessness for about three months on the stairs, carrying loads, and walking fast in cold wind, relieved within minutes by rest; never at rest; no fainting or palpitations. Typical angina by its features. Risk factors: about 25 cigarettes a day since 16 (about 39 pack-years); hazardous drinking (AUDIT 12); LDL cholesterol 168 mg/dL with HDL 38 and triglycerides 200 mg/dL; HbA1c 5.9%; blood pressure 138/86; BMI 28.1. Creatinine 0.98 mg/dL (eGFR 96), potassium 4.4 mmol/L, ALT 41 U/L, hemoglobin 15.8 g/dL, TSH 1.9 mIU/L. Resting ECG: sinus rhythm, no Q waves or ST changes. Breathlessness and weakness on hard exertion during earlier expeditions are part of his history, as is a heart murmur heard by an expedition doctor. Examination today: no murmur, no carotid bruits, lungs clear, no edema. Started today: aspirin 81 mg, atorvastatin 80 mg, metoprolol succinate 50 mg, and sublingual nitroglycerin; varenicline with a quit date in one week; brief alcohol intervention. He is uneasy about examinations and worried that a diagnosis will stop the expedition; he agreed to the referral after his concerns were discussed, and asks that nothing be shared with the expedition's backers without his consent
questions: Does he have obstructive coronary disease, and what is the best first test?
Is the heart murmur heard in the past, or a structural problem, part of the picture?
How should his medical therapy be optimized?
Does he need revascularization, and what would it offer him?
Is he fit to lead a remote polar expedition in four months, and what precautions are needed?

consultant_note.history: Mr. Shackleton, a 47-year-old expedition leader, is seen at the request of Dr. Ellingsworth-Daly for three months of exertional chest tightness and breathlessness. Since starting metoprolol two weeks ago the episodes are less frequent but still come two or three times a week on stairs or with a load and pass within three minutes of rest; nitroglycerin has relieved them twice. There is no rest pain, syncope, palpitations, orthopnea, or ankle swelling. He stopped smoking a week ago. He sails in about four months on a long voyage with port calls and weeks at sea far from a hospital, and expects heavy physical work in cold conditions. He wants to lead the expedition and is frank that he would rather not know of anything that could stop him; we agreed that he would hear everything and make the decisions himself
consultant_note.data_reviewed: Dr. Ellingsworth-Daly's intake note and results: LDL cholesterol 168 mg/dL, HDL 38, triglycerides 200, total cholesterol 246 mg/dL; HbA1c 5.9%; creatinine 0.98 mg/dL; resting ECG normal. Today: coronary CT angiography with a calcium score of 210, an 80% mixed plaque in the proximal left anterior descending artery with a CT-derived fractional flow reserve of 0.70 distal to it, a 30% plaque in the mid right coronary artery, and no left main disease. Transthoracic echocardiogram: normal left ventricular size and wall motion, LVEF 58%, normal valves, normal right heart, and no interatrial shunt on color Doppler or the agitated-saline study

assessment.display: Chronic coronary disease with stable exertional angina
assessment.assessment: His typical exertional angina and risk factors gave an intermediate-to-high pretest probability. Coronary CT angiography is a recommended first test at his age and gives the anatomy. It shows a flow-limiting proximal LAD stenosis (CT-FFR 0.70), which explains the angina, with nonobstructive right coronary disease and normal left ventricular function. Without left main disease or a reduced ejection fraction, revascularization in chronic coronary disease improves angina and quality of life but has not been shown to lower the risk of death or heart attack compared with optimized medical therapy. The first step is therefore a higher beta-blocker dose. If angina persists, angiography and a stent to the LAD are reasonable, by shared decision, with dual antiplatelet therapy for six months after an elective stent

assessment.display: Past heart murmur and episodes of exertional breathlessness
assessment.assessment: There is no murmur today, and the echocardiogram shows normal valves, a normal right heart, and no interatrial shunt, so there is no structural explanation such as an atrial septal defect. The present picture is fully explained by the coronary disease

assessment.display: Fitness for a remote polar expedition
assessment.assessment: If he is free of angina on treatment and a symptom-limited exercise test shows good capacity without ischemia, he can sail with precautions. The main risks are an acute coronary event far from a catheter laboratory, bleeding on dual antiplatelet therapy after injury, and the extra cardiac demand of cold and heavy work. Stopping smoking is the single most important change he can make

recommendations: Increase metoprolol succinate to 100 mg daily; continue aspirin 81 mg, atorvastatin 80 mg, and sublingual nitroglycerin
Lipid panel 4 to 12 weeks after starting the statin; add ezetimibe if LDL cholesterol is 55 mg/dL or higher

Review in four weeks: if angina persists, invasive coronary angiography by the radial artery with a drug-eluting stent to the proximal LAD, after a shared decision, then aspirin with clopidogrel for six months and aspirin alone after
Cardiac rehabilitation, and supervised exercise before the voyage
Continue varenicline with counseling; no smoking at sea

Before departure: a symptom-limited exercise ECG; a written cardiac summary and medicines with spares; a defibrillator and emergency cardiac medicines aboard; satellite access to cardiology; an evacuation plan to cardiac centers at the ports; and advice on cold stress
No routine surveillance stress testing or imaging afterward; test again only if symptoms change
consultant_note.communication: Discussed with Dr. Ellingsworth-Daly, who saw him the same day. The results and options were explained to Mr. Shackleton with the images, and he agreed with the plan. As he asked, nothing will be shared with his backers without his consent
consultant_note.follow_up: Cardiology review after the primary-care visit in four weeks, to decide on angiography; pre-departure review with the exercise test result
